name: Whole-Bible Reading Plans (Discipline)

objectives.text: Recall that the Bible has two main parts called the Old Testament and the New Testament
Identify Genesis as the first book and Revelation as the last book and explain that the Bible tells one story from beginning to end
Retell in order the major stories heard as an adult reads through a picture Bible from creation to the early church
Name the four Gospels and explain that they tell the story of Jesus so that people may believe in him
Sort the books of the Bible into their divisions such as Law, History, Poetry, Prophets, Gospels, Letters, and Prophecy
Locate any book of the Bible quickly using the table of contents and knowledge of its division
Summarize the storyline of the whole Bible from creation and fall through redemption in Christ to the new heavens and new earth
Use a reading plan to read one entire book of the Bible from start to finish while recording each completed reading
Explain from Scripture why the Reformed tradition teaches that God's people should read the whole counsel of God rather than only favorite verses
Compare the length, genre, and reading pace of different books such as Psalms and Mark to estimate the time a reading plan requires
Describe how Israel publicly read the whole law to all the people using examples from Deuteronomy and Nehemiah
Analyze how canonical, chronological, and multi-stream reading plans are structured and what each emphasizes
Describe the Reformed practice of lectio continua as reading consecutively through whole books of Scripture in worship and at home
Explain the directions the Westminster Standards give for how Scripture is to be read and apply them to keeping a long reading plan
Connect each book read in a plan to its place in the larger storyline of Scripture
Trace how the Old Testament prepares the way for Christ and the New Testament across a whole-Bible reading
Explain the Reformed principle that Scripture interprets Scripture and how reading the whole Bible equips a reader to apply it
Evaluate the strengths and weaknesses of historic and modern reading plans such as M'Cheyne, chronological, and canonical plans
Develop strategies for reading difficult portions such as genealogies, laws, and prophecies within a plan using the confessional teaching that not all Scripture is equally plain
Construct a personalized plan to read the entire Bible in one or two years with daily portions, pacing, and a catch-up strategy
Evaluate a completed reading record to identify neglected portions of the canon and revise a plan to cover them
Produce a written synthesis of a major biblical theme traced through a whole-Bible reading

changes: Kept and reworded the real competencies (two testaments, first and last books, Gospels, book divisions, storyline summary, finishing a book, comparing books, plan structures, metanarrative, whole counsel, Old Testament preparing for the New, evaluating plans, constructing a plan, theme synthesis). Merged the whole counsel objective into a grade 6 explanation with its scriptural and confessional basis. Dropped the independent historical research objective as belonging to inductive study and comprehension siblings. Added navigation of the canon, Israel's public reading of the whole law, the Reformed practice of lectio continua, the Westminster directions for reading, Scripture interpreting Scripture, strategies for difficult portions, and auditing a reading record for neglected parts. Replaced the confession citation with precise articles (WCF 1.2, 1.6, 1.7, 1.9, 7.5-6, 21.5, WSC Q90, WLC Q156-157, Belgic 4) and added verse-level scripture anchors.
